Hi Mina,

Thanks for the call last week. We're formalizing requirements for a private Redwood deployment (VPC + private control plane). The networking/security team asked for a short write-up comparing three connectivity options: VPC Peering (cross-account), AWS PrivateLink (interface endpoints), and site-to-site VPN. Key concerns:

- How each option affects blast radius and routing exposure across accounts
- Egress and cross-AZ data transfer cost implications (ballpark)
- Auditability (flow logs, per-tenant access logging) and where TLS terminates
- Multi-region support for an initial us-west/us-east roll-out
- Operational overhead: certs, key rotation, reconnection SLAs

I've attached our RFP snippet with their networking checklist. Can Redwood provide a short comparison and a recommended path for an initial POC vs production? Also please include any procurement or compliance artifacts we'd need to complete (SOC2 evidence, network diagrams, sample SLA language).

Appreciate it — Priya

Hi Priya — thanks for the clear list. Looping in Ben (networking) and Connor (security/compliance) so we can give a tight, operational answer. High level (short):

- PrivateLink (interface endpoints): strongest isolation model — traffic never appears in your VPC route tables to our VPC, good for least-privilege and PCI/HIPAA patterns. Slightly higher per-request cost (endpoint data processing) but easier for teams that cannot allow cross-account CIDR overlap. Works across AZs; cross-region requires an endpoint per-region or use of a regional load balancer.

- VPC Peering (cross-account): lowest per-byte cost and minimal latency. But it expands routing visibility and requires careful CIDR planning — not great if you need strict tenancy separation or have multiple overlapping CIDRs. Peering also scales poorly for many small customer VPCs.

- Site-to-site VPN: good for POC or limited traffic. Less predictable latency/cost, harder to meet aggressive SLOs for high-throughput inference. Simplest to stand up, but increases operational burden (tunnels, key rotation).

We can send a compact matrix with latency/cost/operational trade-offs and a recommended default for production. My initial recommendation: PrivateLink for first-production rollout where compliance and minimal routing exposure matter; consider peering only if you need sustained high throughput and you can commit to dedicated CIDR planning/peering governance. VPN as POC/backup.

Can you share expected concurrent QPS, average token throughput, and whether CedarPoint requires traffic egress to leave your VPC (i.e., do you want inference results to route back over the same private path)? That will change the sizing and cost numbers.

Proposed next step: 30-min technical call Monday to review the matrix and an example mutual action plan. I added Ben and Connor to the invite options below.

— Mina

Priya / team — following up with the technical matrix I promised. Below is a concise trade-off list and an operational checklist for each option. Quoting Mina's summary above for context.

--- trade-offs (brief) ---
1) PrivateLink (interface endpoints)
  - Isolation: High (endpoint in customer VPC forwards to our private NLB in Redwood accounts)
  - Routing exposure: None (no route table exchanges required)
  - Latency: +5–15ms overhead vs peering depending on NLB placement and AZ alignment
  - Cost: Endpoint data processing + data transfer (moderate). Example: for 10TB/month, expect ~USD 700–1,200 extra vs peering (very rough).
  - Operational: Requires provisioning an Interface Endpoint per region; certs handled by Redwood; cross-account IAM policy for endpoint service.
  - Logs/Audit: VPC Flow Logs + PrivateLink flow logs at customer side; Redwood provides request traces and token-level billing in Console.

2) VPC Peering (cross-account)
  - Isolation: Lower (route propagation into your VPC routes)
  - Routing exposure: High — must coordinate CIDR and route table rules; any lateral access must be restricted via security groups & NACLs.
  - Latency: Best (lowest additional latency)
  - Cost: Lowest per-GB egress for sustained traffic.
  - Operational: Peering established once; scaling pain if you have many customer VPCs. Peering doesn't support transitive routing.
  - Logs/Audit: VPC Flow Logs (customer side) + Redwood request traces; more burden on customer to filter traffic flows.

3) Site-to-site VPN
  - Isolation: Medium (endpoint sits at the boundary; still traverses customer gateway)
  - Routing exposure: Medium — depends on tunnel config and split-tunnel choice
  - Latency: Variable and often higher; jitter depends on ISP links
  - Cost: Low setup cost but higher ops cost (maintaining tunnels/ASAs); bandwidth costs on your side can be significant for sustained traffic
  - Operational: Use for POC, DR, or low-throughput environments. Not recommended for heavy production inference unless you accept higher SLO variability.

--- checklist for CedarPoint (what we'll need) ---
- Target CIDR ranges per VPC/region (for peering)
- Desired endpoint placement (single AZ vs multi-AZ) and expected average & peak QPS
- Compliance profile: do you need private endpoints for egress (no internet egress) and are there any regional data residency constraints?
- Contact info for networking ops for peering/endpoint setup

I've attached a CSV matrix with a simple scoring (latency, cost, ops, compliance) and a ballpark pricing workbook. We'll also include an example CloudFormation snippet for a PrivateLink endpoint service if you want to self-provision the customer-side endpoint.

[Attachment: connectivity_matrix.csv (CSV, 1 sheet)]
[Attachment: redwood-pricing-ballpark.xlsx (XLSX, 1 sheet)]

Ben Carter

Thanks, team — super helpful. A few clarifying items before our call: 

1) TLS termination: We prefer TLS to terminate on our side (the client terminates; Redwood to accept mTLS at the endpoint). Does PrivateLink support mTLS to Redwood's NLB, or do you terminate TLS at Redwood and re-encrypt?
2) Multi-region: we plan active-active between us-west-2 and us-east-1 eventually. If we use PrivateLink, do we need an endpoint in each region plus cross-region DNS failover?
3) Audit logs: our security team needs a per-request idempotent trace that ties requests back to our user IDs. Can Redwood surface a request id header in logs and retention of logs (90 days)?
4) Procurement: can you share a minimal mutual action plan (MAP) — procurement steps, required contract language for data handling, and estimated timeline for a paid POC?

If you can answer 1–3 in the call, we can hammer the MAP and get procurement started. Also sent a short questionnaire to procurement; happy to share it after the call.

Jared/Priya — quick summary before our 30-min call (proposed 16:00 PT today) and to answer the bullets so procurement has something to act on.

1) TLS termination and mTLS: PrivateLink supports end-to-end TLS. Our standard pattern: client <-> customer endpoint (mTLS optional) <-> AWS PrivateLink interface endpoint <-> Redwood NLB with TLS. We can support client-provided certs (mTLS) at the PrivateLink service level via AWS ACM and additional mutual-auth steps, or we can terminate at Redwood and re-encrypt the backend path. For highest assurance, we recommend mTLS from your client to the endpoint. We'll provide an example ACM-based configuration and CSR guidance in the drive link.

2) Multi-region: Yes, you'll need an interface endpoint per region where you want local access. For active-active, we recommend DNS-based failover with health checks (Route53 latency-based or weighted records). We can also offer cross-region replication of model endpoints but that is a separate config item.

3) Auditing & retention: Redwood emits a request-id header for every call and records per-request metadata in our Console and the audit logs. Standard retention on hosted audit trails is 90 days; we can extend retention as an add-on or provide S3 export for longer retention windows for compliance. We'll document the header name (X-Redwood-ReqId) and the mapping to logs before procurement.

4) MAP and procurement: attached is a one-page Mutual Action Plan template that outlines milestones (POC kickoff, security review, production cutover), docs we need (SOC2 attestation, network diagrams, encryption/key rotation policy), and an estimated 6–8 week timeline for a paid POC once contracts are signed. We can expedite to 3–4 weeks for a focused POC with a single-region PrivateLink path.

- Redwood: provide ACM CSR guidance, PrivateLink CloudFormation snippet, and MAP/contract summary (Mina/Ben/Connor) — due Thu 17:00 PT
- Both: 16:00 PT call today to confirm technical details and sign off on MAP draft
